body: Paul Brown’s 1990 essay “Beyond Art”, published in 21C, envisions the impact of information technology on the art world. It anticipates collaboration between artists and emerging technologies like supercomputing and artificial intelligence. Brown also speculates on a direct link between the brain and computers, emphasizing artists' role in shaping this interaction. The essay also calls for computer art to usher in a new era of democratization in art, offering an optimistic contrast to much of the pessimism surrounding computer art to close out the decade.

body: “The 1990s witnessed a technological development of unprecedented speed for the digital medium—the so-called ‘digital revolution.’”
-Christiane Paul in Digital Art (2003)
The eminent Paul attributes this revolution to two factors: 1. Hardware and software improvements and affordability 2. The birth of the Internet

Many of these hardware and software developments occurred in our previous chapter on the ’80s. These include the release affordable PCs like Apple’s Macintosh and the Commodore 64 as well as software like Macromedia Director.
[For more context, we suggest youtube.com or open.spotify.com (transcript) to our Ch 7 Artist Discussion with Auriea Harvey⁠, ⁠Joshua Davis⁠, ⁠LIA⁠, ⁠Scott Draves⁠ and ⁠Vuk Ćosić⁠⁠.]
But the Internet, or this early public version called the World Wide Web, was a ’90s phenomena as Paul said.

We begin the decade slightly out of order at the end of 1990 instead of the beginning. We make this choice to emphasize the looming paradigm shift that is the Internet. It would come to dominate the rest of the decade and that, of course, was only the beginning.

For art itself and our story, the Internet not only brought us net.art, which we discuss at length in this chapter beginning in the middle part of the decade, but it also enabled the continued rise of mass-media art. This is the idea that art could be produced in infinite quantities and distributed globally in an instant. The rise of mass-media art can be seen as a theme throughout this decade, where artists, enabled by the Internet, could share their work globally in an instant. The ramifications that would have on art and the art world would be immense. The Internet has changed so much in our lives, it’s easy to forget how much it has also changed art.

By the end of the first year of the decade, Christmas 1990, Berners-Lee, with Robert Cailliau and Nicola Pellow, had created all of the tools required for a functional Web, including HyperText Transfer Protocol (HTTP), HyperText Markup Language (HTML), the first Web browser (WorldWideWeb), the first HTTP server software, the first web server (info.cern.ch), and the first Web pages that described the project itself.
The project would be compiled in its entirety and debuted just a few days later in January, 1991. Just as our decade begins, a foundational shift in human history occurs.

body: This standout generative film by the icon Sims depicted an artificial world and remains an example of an early animation born from artificial evolution. Sims’s work with artificial life can also be thought of as a continuation in the development of AI art. It inspired the work later in this decade of Scott Draves, a machine-learning art pioneer, and many others.

This evolutionary work of Sims can be considered proto-machine learning art. According to Sims: “This botanical form of life, reproducing itself from planet to planet through space, is in many ways analogous to other self replicating systems including organisms, entire species, or even ideas.” These evolving, breeding features of the program—drawn directly from cybernetics and its feedback loops—are the predecessors of machines processing data to perform instructionless tasks, modern machine learning.

As for Panspermia itself, Sims created the piece using original software, in which he created a virtual universe teeming with 3D organic plant structures. Employing chaos, complexity and self-replication, the animation mirrors the biological world, suggesting life’s interstellar distribution through spores. Dynamic simulations and particle systems animated these digital life forms, displaying Sims’s self-propagating systems. Panspermia not only showcases the potential of artificial evolution in computer graphics but also prompts contemplation about life’s interconnectedness and propagation on a planetary scale.
Thomas Dreher describes it as such in History of Computer Art:

“Karl Sims presents in the short film “Panspermia” an artificial world of biological forms as an autonomous cosmos with recurring parallels to the evolution of geology and fauna on earth” [Dreher 180].

This major work by the legendary Sims continues to influence the work of generative artists today (ciphrd) but had a profound impact on the decade of the ’90s and the rise of artificial intelligence art.

img.credit: Courtesy of artist.

body: The final major trend we begin this chapter with is the rise of the demoscene. Cracking, which refers to the removal of a game’s copyright and duplication mechanisms, was a practice that began shortly after video games existed in the late ‘70 and early ’80s. What began with Crackers and Cracktros (programming, pirating and video game hobbyists who programmed introductions to cracked video games in groups) in the ’80s eventually branched off into the demoscene by the late ’80s. This split is believed to be the result of an interest in programming and creativity in the demoscene over piracy and questionably legal activities. Once certain groups such as Future Crew began producing more and more advanced mega-demos, which were strings of intros linked together, the demoscene began to more clearly distinguish itself. It wasn’t until the 1990s that the demoscene truly took off, however. To characterize the demoscene as entirely breaking from its cracker roots would be inaccurate, yet two groups, as we know of them today, did form. Crackers continue to focus on piracy to this day, which demosceners became much more interested in the technical skill of creative programming. The demoscene’s relevance to algorithmic art should be abundantly clear with this following quote from Jim “Trixter” Leonard a few years later in 1994:

“Around this time, a gradual shift occurred, from people cracking games to writing graphic/sound demonstrations that showed off the computer they had just learned to program. Sure, cracking games was still popular, but some people decided that learning about the machine and using it as a tool for creativity was cooler” than cracking one dime-store game after another.”

body: In Feb 1990, Adobe Photoshop, the ground-breaking image editing program, was made public. It changed the digital art world by providing strong tools for graphic design and photo manipulation. Creatives loved its potential, allowing for complex editing and visual storytelling. Photoshop has become a design studio staple and an indispensable tool for artists worldwide, affecting how visual information is generated and altered. The software’s constant progress has left an unmistakable effect on generative art, allowing creators to realize their visionary projects with unparalleled accuracy and originality.

body: A monumentally important figure, Kawaguchi is a pioneer of computer 3D graphics and of procedural artificial-life work.

Heralded in Frank Popper’s Art of the Electronic Age, this example of the legendary growth algorithm by Kawaguchi stands out in the algorithm’s evolution. According to Popper, “The light, aided by the sophisticated technology of ray tracing recalls the art of Japanese lacquer or porcelain.” [Popper 88]
The same year, Kawaguchi spoke to SIGGRRAPH, saying:
“My pieces are being carried out on a paradigm that ‘growth model is created by the recursive structure of the self-organization, thus being the fruit of complexed form of evolutional cells.’”
Kawaguchi’s growth models, first presented at SIGGRAPH in 1982, are a procedural precursor to later artificial-life and AI art rather than machine learning themselves.

body: Mentioned in Frank Popper’s Art of the Electronic Age, Latham’s work showcased his Mutator algorithm, combining chance mutations with creative choices to produce ever-evolving 3D forms of enormous complexity.

The work is actually a collaboration with Latham’s long-time collaborator Stephen Todd. Latham and Todd began working on the revolutionary generative art system, Mutator Evolutionary Art, together with a team at IBM beginning in 1987. Besides Latham and Todd, the team included Lance Putnam and Peter Todd. Their work displayed “strange organic, often serpentine, forms, produced using [an] “alternative evolutionary software system” (developed with Stephen Todd and team), which William uses to pick and breed 3D forms freed from the limits of the human imagination.”
Latham and Todd collaborated on Mutator and FormGrow between 1987 and 1993 so this piece marks a middle-point in their time creating together.

This evolutionary work of Latham and Todd can be considered proto-machine learning art, as the evolving, breeding features of the program—drawn directly from cybernetics and its feedback loops—are the predecessors of machines processing data to perform instructionless tasks, modern machine learning.
There is even an image of Latham working on this very piece.

body: As we begin the 1990s, a major trend, besides the rise of the Internet and the transition from “computer” to “digital” art, was a fascination with virtual reality. Focusing on virtual reality, the first ArtFutura, a now annual festival of digital culture, was held at Mercat de les Flors in Barcelona, marking a significant milestone in the realm of art and technology. The event showcased a one-hour projection and a 30-minute performance titled Mugra, a collaboration between Rebecca Allen and La Fura dels Baus. It was a very early attempt at virtual reality and art. A memorable moment was Eric Gullichsen’s presentation of a virtual reality helmet during the press conference, allowing journalists to experience real-time 3D environments. The event even included an early 3D animation from the little-known Pixar animation studio.

body: This pioneering idea in machine learning during the supposed “AI winter” was a proposal of a generative adversarial network (GAN), which would not be formally realized until 2014. This was an example of an important development in the creative application of neural networks, demonstrating how far-reaching the ideas of the past decade-plus extend. The framework involved two competing neural networks: a generator (controller) that creates outputs and a predictor (world model) that anticipates the consequences of these outputs. The networks engage in a minimax game, where the generator aims to maximize the predictor’s error, while the predictor minimizes it. This early concept laid the groundwork for future developments in generative models, including the now widely used Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs).

body: This book stands as a survey of the field of the creative application of neural networks to create music. The work expounds the early work of David Cope from 1981 and Todd’s own earlier ideas. This includes Todd’s influential work, “A Connectionist Approach to Algorithmic Composition,” (1989) in which he describes some of the earliest creative application of the ability to “generalize” from data rather than follow programmed rules. Todd explains how a: “fundamental shift allows the development of new algorithmic composition methods that rely on learning the structure of existing musical examples and generalizing from these learned structures to compose new pieces. These methods contrast greatly with the majority of older schemes that simply follow a previously assembled set of compositional rules.” The book’s research introduced parallel distributed processing (PDP) to the field of music composition, which allowed for the generation of new musical pieces based on learned structures from existing examples. As Todd explained, this approach marked a significant shift from rule-based methods to a more dynamic, self-learning system.

body: January 1991 the first Web servers outside CERN itself were switched on. On August 6, 1991, Berners-Lee posted a short summary of the World Wide Web project on the alt.hypertext newsgroup. This date also marked the debut of the Web as a publicly available service on the Internet. While CERN would not place the Web software in the public domain until 30 April 1993, this event twenty months earlier ushered in a new era of information accessibility. Tim Berners-Lee’s idea unleashed a rush of digital inventiveness, as within just a few years of even this launch, artists would be making the first net art. This would of course impact programmatic art, as much of the later part of the decade was spent creating the early tooling (e.g., ACU, DBN) for visual creatives and not computer scientists. As previously mentioned, the Web propelled the rise of mass-media art, but it also represented the democratization of online spaces, which would fuel generative art by allowing creators all over the globe to share their thoughts, cooperate across borders and alter the bounds of artistic expression in the digital age.

body: In the early ’90s, Sun Microsystems began the development of the Java programming language, a watershed moment in the history of creative coding as it would be the basis for the upcoming Processing in ten years. This versatile and platform-independent language intended for network computing would transform much more than digital generative art, however. The project, led by James Gosling and Mike Sheridan, aimed to develop a language that could run on a variety of devices, ranging from small embedded systems to large-scale business servers. Java would subsequently revolutionize web development with its “Write Once, Run Anywhere” attitude, cementing its place as a cornerstone of modern software development.

body: Roman Verostko, noted for his pioneering work such as The Magic Hand of Chance (1982), organized the Art & Algorithm Symposium at the Minneapolis College of Art and Design in 1991 (February 23-24). This was key proto-Algorist event, named “Mind & Machine,” celebrating the intersection of art and computational techniques. With a name juxtaposing words like “mind” and “machine” in early 1991, along with the work of evolutionary art pioneers like Sims and Latham at the time, this can be seen as proto-artificial intelligence art event. The conference included an audio-visual exhibition titled “Images of the Unseen From the Worlds of Art & Science,” which showcased works by 23 artists and scientists from six nations. Among them are pioneers such as Vera Molnár (Algorithmic drawing, 1990), Donna Cox, Char Davies, Samia Halaby, Hans Dehlinger, Mark Wilson, Jean Pierre Hebert, Yoichiro Kawaguchi and William Latham.

body: Keith Tyson revolutionized the art world with ArtMachine in 1991, which he would work on for the next ten years. Born from the mind of the artist, then in his early twenties, this semi-computerized algorithm scanned the world’s information sources, generating unique “iterations”—artistic directives that Tyson translated into tangible creations. In other words, the system generated proposed artworks for Tyson to make. The ridiculousness of its plans was matched by their literal implementation, ranging from an artwork made of 366 painted breadboards to a “scubasculpture” kept on the bottom of the ocean for sixteen years. Tyson left the creative choices up to ArtMachine in one of the most important examples of material generative art since Cohen’s AARON, particularly from a mainstream, Turner Prize-winning contemporary artist.

body: Included by Frank Popper in Art of the Electronic Age as an important exhibition in the development of electronic art [Popper 14], this exposition focused on works inspired by neon lighting. Held at the Centre National Art and Technologie (CNAT), Les Artistes et la Lumiere (Artists and Light) in Reims, France, this worldwide exposition featured the bright creations of 18 artists from around the world. From neon to lasers, holograms to LEDs, the exhibition celebrated the relationship between light and artistic expression. Aiming to spark interest in light-based art, a key predecessor of digital art, artists included Liliane Lijn, Bill Bell and Pierre-Alain Hubert.

body: The humble coffee pot sparked a technological revolution when computer scientists at the University of Cambridge invented the world’s first webcam. Quentin Stafford-Fraser and Paul Jardetzky built the internal XCoffee camera system in 1991 to monitor the elusive coffee levels in the Trojan Room, their lab’s main computer room. Daniel Gordon and Martyn Johnson later rebuilt it with a new frame grabber and put the images on the World Wide Web on 22 November 1993, making it the first webcam. From the commonplace coffee pot, an era of video chats and live webcasts emerged, forever altering human-machine communication and interaction.

body: One of four similar works in a series, this piece was included by Frank Popper in Art of the Electronic Age. Joan Truckenbrod’s Sociotecture series, initiated in 1991, explored the unseen dimensions of the human experience. Informed by the mythology of Native American beliefs in animating spirits, Truckenbrod’s algorithmic images embody these invisible forces. The series gradually evolves, mixing mathematical symbols within a natural ecology of leaves and flower petals. The project was inspired by emotional echoes of Gertrude Stein, John Cage’s avant-garde methods and Pierre Boulez and George Benjamin’s compositions.
Truckenbrod herself wrote of the work:

“To create my early algorithmic images I created my own personal geometry that embodied these animating spirits. Coding was a vehicle for giving form to algebraic formulas that scientifically describes invisible forces such as how light waves reflect off of irregular surfaces.”

body: A member of Jeffrey Steele’s Systems Group (1969) and a former member of the British Constructivists, Wise was a prominent example of a systems artist, like Vera Molnar, moving from systematic thinking to programmed art with computers. This work was made by creating color computerized images with symmetrical forms and is featured in Frank Popper’s Art of the Electronic Age. Wise continued working with material forms throughout her career as well.

body: The Virtual Museum by Jeffrey Shaw emerged in Frankfurt, Germany, as a pioneering exploration of virtual reality. With hardware by Huib Nelissen and software by Gideon May, this three-dimensional computer-generated museum marked a conceptual shift in exhibiting immaterial artistic creations. Viewers engaged in interactive journeys, controlling their movement through a circular, rotating platform with a large video projection monitor. The Virtual Museum featured five rooms, deemphasizing differences between real and virtual spaces that are now commonplace but were much more radical in 1991. In this sense, like many of these early-90s VR displays, it can be seen as a proto-Metaverse. Exhibited globally, it left a undeniable mark on the evolving landscape of virtual art, contributing to exhibitions in Frankfurt, Paris, Nagoya, Linz, Munich, Madrid, Los Angeles, Hannover, San José, Madrid, Valladolid, Reykjavik, Hengelo, Shanghai, Zagreb, Karlsruhe, and beyond.

img.credit: Courtesy of artist.

body: Made between 1989 and 1990, the work by Monika Fleischmann and Wolfgang Strauss is described by the artists as the first artistic virtual reality installation. Participants, equipped with VPL Datagloves, could enter and explore the spaces of images by moving their feet, hands and head in Proto-Metaverse, immerse VR environment popular at the time.
The following year, the project would go on to receive the Golden Nica at the Prix Ars Electronica in 1992.

body: Carolina Cruz-Neira, Daniel J. Sandin and Thomas A. DeFanti, with Robert V. Kenyon and John C. Hart, pioneered the development of the “CAVE” (Cave Automatic Virtual Environment) in the Electronic Visualization Laboratory at the University of Illinois in Chicago beginning in 1991. They would continue development until 1993. This surround-screen, surround-sound, projection-based virtual reality (VR) system transformed immersive experiences. The CAVE featured 3D computer graphics projected into a 10'x10'x9' cube, with display screens surrounding the viewer. Users were able to explore the virtual world without wearing helmets thanks to lightweight stereo glasses and a wand-like device. Designed for scientific visualization, the CAVE enabled collaborative exploration and discussions among users, making it a transformative tool for scientific discovery.

body: Karl Sims unveiled this important work in the development of artificial life-based art, Primordial Dance, an experimental one-minute and 35-second code-based animation exploring abstract textures and colors. Sims worked with the computer to generate images and movements that exceeded their individual capabilities through an interactive process known as “artificial evolution.” Sims explains how his “artificial evolution” is essentially a slightly more manual GAN process. There is a clear connection between the AI of today and Sims’s work, as he explains his process himself: “The computer generates and displays a collection of experimental abstract images. The artist chooses the most aesthetically interesting images, and those survive and are “bred” to produce a new collection of images. The equations, or artificial genes, of the survivors are copied, mutated, and mated by the computer to generate new offspring pictures.” Thus, this evolutionary work of Sims can be considered proto-GAN art. Artists in the upcoming decades would continue to automate the process until now these tasks are done “under the hood” and instantly. But this is a hugely important step in the development of AI-art-as-we-know-it-today.

img.credit: Courtesy of Karl Sims.

body: A key moment in the development of blockchain technology and, thus, NFTs, Stuart Haber and W. Scott Stornetta described a cryptographically secure chain of blocks, presented at CRYPTO ’90 and published in 1991. This moment, along with David Chaum’s 1982 dissertation, essentially introduced the concept of blockchain technology. The research would lay the groundwork for what would eventually become blockchain technology. Haber and Stornetta developed a novel method for timestamping digital documents using a cryptographic hash function. This novel approach resulted in an immutable chain of blocks that maintained the integrity and chronological order of digital records. These ideas have obviously become foundational to any blockchain-based activity, including NFTs.

img.cap: A Surety 'Universal Registry Entries' notice circled in red in the classified pages of The New York Times of 19 August 2018 — the weekly published hash chain that has run since 1995 on Haber and Stornetta's scheme. Stuart Haber's conference badge is visible behind the newspaper.
img.credit: Photograph reproduced in 'The First Blockchain, or How to Time-Stamp a Digital Document,' Decentralized Thoughts, 5 July 2020.

body: Similar to the MPEG standard released the same year, the JPEG 1 standard (ISO/IEC 10918) was developed in 1992 as part of an effort to reduce the standard image file size, a process that began in 1986. Though this standard is sometimes referred to as a single specification, it is really made up of four independent components and a combination of coding modes. It’s still in use to this day after a 1994 update.

body: The Moving Picture Experts Group (MPEG) approved the MPEG-1 standard in November 1992, published as ISO/IEC 11172 in 1993, marking a pivotal moment in the history of digital audio and video compression that various groups had been working on for several years. This comprehensive standard, organized into five parts, addressed the growing need for efficient encoding and decoding of multimedia content. MPEG aimed to create a reference standard to overcome technological barriers and ensure the success of digital audio and video.

body: Breeding Forms on the Infinite Plane, an exemplary work of Latham’s evolutionary art, creates biomorphic prints that resemble insect and crustacean forms. Latham collaborated with Stephen Todd to create intricate 3D shapes and textures using an artificial embryology system called Form Grow and an evolution-based search algorithm known as Mutator. This pioneering work, arguably the first computer-mediated evolutionary art, according to Philip Galanter, helped rejuvenate code-based art, sparking a new era of artistic experimentation. Mutator and FormGrow were developed by the pair at IBM on their state of the art mainframes beginning in 1987. The collaboration would only last for one more year in 1993. The work is actually a collaboration with Latham’s long-time collaborator Stephen Todd. Latham and Todd began working on the revolutionary generative art system, Mutator Evolutionary Art, together with a team at IBM beginning in 1987. Besides Latham and Todd, the team included Lance Putnam and Peter Todd. Their work displayed “strange organic, often serpentine, forms, produced using [an] “alternative evolutionary software system” (developed with Stephen Todd and team), which William uses to pick and breed 3D forms freed from the limits of the human imagination.” Latham and Todd collaborated on Mutator and FormGrow between 1987 and 1993 so this piece marks a middle-point in their time creating together. This evolutionary work of Latham and Todd can be considered proto-machine learning art, as the evolving, breeding features of the program—drawn directly from cybernetics and its feedback loops—are the predecessors of machines processing data to perform instructionless tasks, modern machine learning.

cite.label: Todd, Stephen and William Latham. Evolutionary Art and Computers, plate 29. London and San Diego: Academic Press, 1992.

body: William Latham’s Mutations (1991-92) depicts a surreal journey of real-time evolutionary art, showcasing intricate breeding and growth processes through animated forms engaged in complex interactions. This significant work represents a watershed moment in the development of artificial life in the realm of art, providing viewers with a glimpse into a dynamic and evolving world now achievable due to the digital.
Latham’s work showcased his Mutator algorithm, combining chance mutations with creative choices to produce ever-evolving 3D forms of enormous complexity.

The work is actually a collaboration with Latham’s long-time collaborator Stephen Todd. Latham and Todd began working on the revolutionary generative art system, Mutator Evolutionary Art, together with a team at IBM beginning in 1987. Besides Latham and Todd, the team included Lance Putnam and Peter Todd. Their work displayed “strange organic, often serpentine, forms, produced using [an] “alternative evolutionary software system” (developed with Stephen Todd and team), which William uses to pick and breed 3D forms freed from the limits of the human imagination.”
Latham and Todd collaborated on Mutator and FormGrow between 1987 and 1993 so this piece marks a middle-point in their time creating together.

This evolutionary work of Latham and Todd can be considered proto-machine learning art, as the evolving, breeding features of the program—drawn directly from cybernetics and its feedback loops—are the predecessors of machines processing data to perform instructionless tasks, modern machine learning.

body: Described by Arthur I. Miller in Colliding Worlds as an early piece of open-source graphics software, Fractal Flames made Scott Draves one of software art’s most prominent names. The algorithm, a notable addition to the Iterated Function System (IFS) class of fractal algorithms, was, according to Draves, “art out of math.” The work would go on to gain recognition the following year, receiving it honorary mention for the Prix Ars Electronica. The algorithm typified the belief that enabling other community members and artists was important. This became increasingly relevant during the early ’90s when the web was still in its infancy.

The algorithm went viral in mid ’90s as it was used by others artists without needing to credit Draves at all. It was used in an IBM Super Bowl commercial as well as the cover of popular books and albums, including the work of Stephen King and Paul Simon.

img.credit: Wikipedia. 2023. "Scott Draves." Wikimedia Foundation. Last modified December 28, 2023. en.wikipedia.org.

body: Between 1989 and 1992, Stenger worked on Angels, the first immersive movie and an important early VR work. She developed the project at MIT and the University of Washington with an Advanced Visualizer. Users could interact in the space with a VPL Dataglove. This work further demonstrates the popularity of VR as we began the early ’90s. Further, this and similar works can be seen as an emerging “Proto-Metaverse” with direct genealogy to today’s concepts.

img.credit: Wikipedia. 2024. "Nicole Stenger." Wikimedia Foundation. Last modified February 28, 2024. en.wikipedia.org.

body: The winning PC demo of the inaugural Assembly Party, Unreal, marked a significant milestone in the demoscene community. Created by Future Crew, the piece highlighted the creators' innovative talents, as Unreal not only won the Assembly Party, but also laid the groundwork for Future Crew’s evolution into Futuremark, a well-known developer of PC benchmark tests such as 3D Mark and PCMark. Furthermore, key members of the Finnish game developer Remedy emerged from the Future Crew team, demonstrating the demoscene’s interconnectedness to the gaming industry, particularly in the Nordic region.
Results from these early demoscene competitions can still be found online and some of the works can still be played on emulators.

img.credit: Wikipedia. 2023. "Assembly (Demoparty)." Wikimedia Foundation. Last modified December 14, 2023. en.wikipedia.org).

body: Legend I is the first piece in Yoshiyuki Abe’s renowned series, which ran until 2001 and was featured at ISEA94. Abe’s digital creations use a variation of the ray tracing algorithm to display intricate features of hyperbolic paraboloid surfaces in Cartesian coordinates. This innovative approach to “un-normalized” shading results in complex visual compositions. Abe’s extensive knowledge of digital art and technology has cemented his reputation as a leading figure in Japan’s algorithmic and electronic art scenes. Abe’s generative process investigates the use of quadratic parameters to define lighting, surface attributes and colors that appear metallic and gel-like in Legend, evoking the contemporary work of Cyril Diagne.

img.credit: Spalter Digital Collection. Legend I. spalterdigital.com

body: On Justifying the Hypothetical Nature of Art and the Non-Identicality within the Object World at Gallery Tanja Grunert, Cologne, presented an interactive computer installation that immersed visitors into a dark triangular space illuminated only by a large screen, serving as a portal to virtual worlds. By stepping on colored spots on the floor, visitors navigated between real and virtual environments, influencing the appearance and behavior of the digital landscapes. This interactive digital installation challenged perceptions of reality and anticipated the immersive digital work of artists today like Refik Anadol.

body: Another work of Virtual Reality in the early ’90s, Placeholder, a VR initiative by Interval Research Corporation and The Banff Centre for The Performing Arts, was created by Brenda Laurel and Rachel Strickland. The work pioneered multi-person narrative action in virtual environments. Additionally, the publication “Placeholder: Landscape and Narrative In Virtual Environments,” authored by Brenda Laurel, Rachel Strickland and Rob Tow, offers insights into the project’s objectives and achievements. For a visual journey through the project, see Rachel Strickland’s documentary video on Placeholder.

body: This moment stands as one of the earliest predecessors of the big-data, machine-learning AI art of today, as opposed to the symbolic AI art of Harold Cohen. “One of the earliest machine learning image2image algorithm[s],” according to Draves himself, Fuse stands as a critical step in the development of AI art. Scott Draves developed the Fuse algorithm, drawing inspiration from the Dissociated Press and Cut-Up technique. The process worked by slicing and rearranging images into new compositions, predating Efros and Leung’s texture synthesis (1999) and Robert Silvers’s Photomosaics (1995). Released as open source in 1993, Fuse became influential in digital art. Draves' self-portrait, composed of fragmented images, exemplified its creative potential and is one of the earliest examples machine-learning art as we know it. Draves’s work was inspired by the artificial life work of Karl Sims and also can be traced back to the work of William Latham.

img.cap: One of Scott Draves's 1993 Fuse images — photographs of hands sliced and reassembled by the Fuse algorithm — from the artist's own fuse2 gallery of works made that year.
img.credit: Scott Draves, hands3, from the 1993 Fuse gallery. Courtesy of the artist (spot at draves dot org), CC BY-SA 3.0 US.

body: According to Art Historian Frank Popper, by 1993, the term “computer art” had evolved from a distinct category to simply one of many electronic art forms. Grant Taylor’s observations in When the Machine Made Art highlight this shift, citing the emergence of the New York Digital Salon in 1993 as a watershed moment in the transition from “computer” to “digital” art. As discussed, in the previous chapter, the term began falling out of favor in late 1980s. The term was in retreat by 1993, though it remained in institutional use: the New York Digital Salon’s own 1993 founding statement described the venture as a venue for the exhibition of computer art.

img.cap: The front cover of Frank Popper's Art of the Electronic Age, published in 1993 — the book behind the record's claim that 'computer art' had by then become one electronic art form among many.
img.credit: Cover of Frank Popper, Art of the Electronic Age (New York: Harry N. Abrams, 1993). Internet Archive.

body: A-Volve (1993–94) was an interactive-evolutionary art environment that stands as an important step in the development of AI art. For the piece, visitors could draw virtual organisms using a sensor pencil, which then came to life in a water-filled glass pool. These three-dimensional creatures reacted to human behavior, evolving and interacting with each other and the visitors.

This participatory-evolutionary-immersive art display anticipates the work of Karl Sims’s Galapagos in 1997. The algorithmic evolution achieved by Sommerer and Mignonneau also anticipate machine learning and GAN art. The process for the piece worked as follows:

“If two strong creatures meet, they can create an offspring and a new creature can be born. It carries the genetic code of its parents. Mutation and cross-over provides a nature-like reproduction mechanism, that follows the genetic rules of Mendel.“

This evolutionary process is a much more simplified version of the complex learning machines are capable of today. But this early work is a direct predecessor. Artists in the upcoming decades would continue to automate the process until now these tasks are done “under the hood” and instantly. But this is a hugely important step in the development of AI-art-as-we-know-it-today.

Beyond its significance to the development of AI art, the installation blurred the lines between real and unreal, exploring popular themes of generative art at the time: concepts of artificial life and evolution, while adding Sommerer and Mignonneau’s distinct individuality. A-Volve continued the artists' exploration of natural interfaces and complex interactivity, challenging perceptions of reality and creating a dynamic ecosystem where visitors become integral participants in the evolution of artificial life. This would continue into the next decade as well with Life Writer (2006).

img.cap: A-Volve interactive A-Life installation © 1994, Christa Sommerer & Laurent Mignonneau
img.credit: Wikipedia. 2023. "Christa Sommerer Et Laurent Mignonneau." Wikimedia Foundation. Last modified December 31, 2023. fr.wikipedia.org.

body: At Assembly 93 in July 1993, Future Crew debuted Second Reality, a significant demo showcasing cutting-edge 2D and 3D computer graphics rendering. It captivated audiences for 16 minutes and 19 seconds with its synchronized visuals and Skaven and Purple Motion’s techno soundtrack. The demo, which was released to the public in October 1993, became legendary, being hailed as one of the best creations of the early 1990s PC demo scene. Its innovative techniques, such as real-time mesh deformation and ray tracing, cemented its place as a generative art landmark, inspiring countless remixes and leaving an indelible imprint on digital creativity incorporating generativity.

img.credit: Future Crew; original demo screenshot preserved by Pouët Image source.

body: Just This Once is a computer-generative romance novel authored by a Macintosh IIcx computer named “Hal” in collaboration with programmer Scott French. The radical reinterpretation of the novel and authorship challenged literary norms. French, investing $40,000 and 8 years, developed an AI program to mimic Valley of the Dolls novelist Jacqueline Susann’s writing style. Hal’s output, after significant editing, produced the novel’s plot and style. Eventually, legal disputes with Susann’s estate over copyright were settled, leading to its publication by Carol Publishing Group. Despite mixed reviews, it sparked discussions in legal circles on copyright law’s applicability to computer-generated creative works that anticipate and mirror those questions raised today by AI. Just This Once remains a testament to the intersection of technology and literature, blurring the lines of authorship.

img.cap: The title page of the 1993 first edition of Just This Once, reading 'Just This Once / Scott French / A Birch Lane Press Book, Published by Carol Publishing Group'. This is the title page, not the dust jacket.
img.credit: Title page of Scott French, Just This Once (New York: Birch Lane Press / Carol Publishing Group, 1993). Open Library / Internet Archive.

body: The early ’90s fascination with virtual reality continued with an exhibition at none other than the Guggenheim. The Guggenheim Museum’s Virtual Reality: An Emerging Medium was an Intel Digital Education & Arts Program event. Curators were initially uncertain of the shows reception but the exhibition became a sensation, selling out daily and capturing global media attention. Reflecting on art history, it emphasized VR’s profound impact, similar to Renaissance linear perspective. Notable works include Jenny Holzer’s interactive World I and World II, which challenges communication assumptions, and Thomas Dolby’s Virtual String Quartet, which provides dynamic soundscapes. This event highlighted the intense fascination with VR technology in the early ’90s despite being several decades early in terms of a commercially viable product.

img.cap: A frame from the 1993 documentation video of the Guggenheim exhibition, showing the show's introductory wall panel headed 'A Glimpse over the Horizon'.
img.credit: Frank-Ratchye STUDIO for Creative Inquiry, Virtual Reality: An Emerging Medium (1993), exhibition documentation video. Internet Archive, CC BY 4.0.

body: Genetic Images, a groundbreaking media installation conceived by Karl Sims in 1993, explored the concept of interactive evolution within virtual environments. As with his work Panspermia (1990), Genetic Images can also be thought of as proto-AI art. It inspired the work later in this decade of Scott Draves, a machine-learning art pioneer. Displayed on an arc of screens, this installation allowed visitors to actively participate in the evolution of abstract images. By standing on sensors and selecting aesthetically pleasing images, viewers determined which visuals would survive and reproduce, guiding the course of artificial evolution. It was thus an important example of public interactive art as well in the spirit of GRAV. Exhibited at renowned venues like the Centre Georges Pompidou in Paris and Ars Electronica in Linz, Austria, Genetic Images sparked discussions about the intersection of art and technology while challenging traditional notions of creativity and design in some of the mainstream art world’s most prestigious institutions. That is beside the impact it had on the “evolution” of AI art.

img.credit: Courtesy of Karl Sims.

body: All about instruction-based generative art, do it began in 1993 as a conversation and a book of instructions from twelve artists, from which the exhibitions grew. Initiated by Hans Ulrich Obrist in conversation with artists Christian Boltanski and Bertrand Lavier, do it explores the interpretive role of the viewer in generative art, transcending traditional notions of static displays. Each venue hosted unique interpretations, blurring lines between art and daily life. Do it championed audience involvement, fostering dynamic, ever-changing experiences. Unlike conventional exhibitions, it prioritized human interaction over physical artifacts, inviting diverse renditions that engaged with site specificity.

img.credit: Independent Curators International; photographer not identified Image source.

body: “I recall being surprised by how the computer could do so much at the beckon of a few lines of code.” -John Maeda This profound work marks Maeda’s return to computer programming using the PostScript language after a long hiatus. Inspired by his typography teacher’s questions about Maeda’s ultimate motivation in life, Maeda crafted this piece. He made it for the NeXT computer, with the piece itself featuring an infinite loop, symbolizing the endless potential of digital creation. This concept would appear in future books, such as How To Speak Machine (2019). Maeda halted the drawing at the 10,000th loop stroke. This work not only represents a pivotal moment in Maeda’s career but also reflects his journey from aspiring classical typographer to digital pioneer. AI Infinity holds deep personal significance, illustrating the convergence of his artistic and technological passions.

img.cap: John Maeda's AI Infinity: the accumulated stroke of an infinite loop written in PostScript, halted after 10,000 passes, as published on the artist's own studio site.
img.credit: John Maeda, AI Infinity. Courtesy of the artist, MAEDASTUDIO.

body: Muriel Cooper’s Information Landscapes Project, made with David Small and six others, featured in MoMA’s collection and unveiled at a 1994 TED talk, represented a pinnacle in her illustrious career. Information Landscapes defied traditional graphic design paradigms, exemplifying over four decades of research and experimentation. Cooper, a pioneering figure at MIT, reshaped design education with her visionary approach, founding the Visible Language Workshop in the Bauhaus tradition and designing the iconic MIT Press Logo. Her projects, such as Typography in Space and Personalized Galaxies of Information, celebrated multidimensionality and encouraged viewers to engage actively and explore nonlinearly.

Cooper legacy continued beyond her time, which unfortunately passed shortly after this talk, as John Maeda was the direct descendant of Cooper’s traditions at the VLW. He would found the Aesthetics and Computation Group at the MIT Media Lab, where students Ben Fry and Casey Reas developed Processing.

img.cap: Installation view of Information Landscapes projected at the Museum of Modern Art for Inbox: Muriel Cooper's Information Landscapes, 2016 — three-dimensional typography flying over a mapped landscape labelled 'Cambridge'.
img.credit: Muriel Cooper, David Small, Suguru Ishizaki, Earl Rennison, Robert Silvers, Lisa Strausfeld, Jeffrey Ventrella, Yin Yin Wong. Information Landscapes. 1994. Multimedia video and software with audio. Installation view, The Museum of Modern Art, May 13–June 12, 2016. Gift of Lisa Strausfeld and David Small. Photo: John Wronn.

body: This is an early example of art built on artificial neural networks, although the networks were evolved by genetic algorithms rather than trained on data. The work stands as one of the most significant links from the rule-based AI of Cohen to “Modern AI art,” relying on the evaluation of trained data. The work showcased the evolution of virtual block creatures through simulated Darwinian processes. These creatures were tested on their abilities to perform tasks such as swimming, jumping, and competing. The most successful ones had their virtual genes copied, combined,and mutated to create a new generation. This iterative process led to the emergence of increasingly adept creatures. The project was a continuation and further demonstration of the potential of evolutionary algorithms in artificial life, demonstrating how virtual entities could evolve complex behaviors over successive generations. Sims' work remains influential in the fields of computer graphics and artificial life along with pioneers Yoichioro Kawaguchi, William Latham and Christa Sommerer.

img.cap: Three evolved swimming creatures from Karl Sims's Evolved Virtual Creatures (1994), from the artist's own page on the work.
img.credit: Karl Sims, Evolved Virtual Creatures, 1994. Courtesy of the artist, karlsims.com.

body: This open exhibition premiered in 1994 at the Ritter Kunsthalle in Klagenfurt after its conceptual roots were laid the previous year. Begun by Hans Ulrich Obrist with Christian Boltanski and Bertrand Lavier, the first do it featured instruction-based work by artists such as Mike Kelley, Alison Knowles, Rirkrit Tiravanija, Jean-Jacques Rullier and Bertrand Lavier. The exhibitions were meant to encourage audience participation and interaction.

img.cap: An archival photograph from Independent Curators International's do it archive: a public do it event in a Central European square, with orange balloons printed 'do it'. ICI publishes the photograph without a caption or date, so it cannot be confirmed as the 1994 Klagenfurt exhibition.
img.credit: Independent Curators International, do it archive.

body: The IBM Simon Personal Communicator, a handheld mobile device with a touchscreen is often hailed as the first true smartphone, making its debut in the United States. Distributed by BellSouth Cellular Corp., it sold 50,000 units between August 1994 and February 1995. Combining PDA features with mobile capabilities, the Simon offered functionalities such as faxing, emailing and cellular paging. Despite its innovative design, it faced challenges due to a short battery life and the rise of sleeker flip phones. The Simon’s legacy lies in pioneering the integration of communication and computing, setting the stage for the future of mobile technology. One of Casey Reas’s pre conditions for NFTs is supercomputers in our pockets with high res screens. Like many things that impact our lives so much today, it began in the mid-90s.

In the spring of 1995, Nettime, a mailing list and platform that was instrumental in the formation of net.art, formed. The list gathered the earliest net.art practitioners and was where the term took hold. It consisted of JODI’s Joan Heemskerk and Dirk Paesmans, Geert Lovink, Heath Bunting, Vuk Ćosić and Alexei Shoulgin.

Organized by Geert Lovink and Pit Schultz, Nettime as a group met in June at the Venice Biennale, laying the foundation for what was to come. By fall, nettime-l had taken root, fostering the exchange of ideas and discourse and some of the earliest net.art. Ćosić explained to the author (Peter Bauman) how in his view JODI were the first net.art practitioners:

“On the nettime list itself we didn’t post net.art pieces that could be displayed or collected but we spoke about it and gave it life. I personally adored the JODI posts that were consistently pushing the idea of net.art as a liberating force. They were the first in many regards.”

img.cap: The cover of README!, the nettime reader published by Autonomedia in 1999 — a print anthology filtered from the nettime-l mailing list that formed in 1995. It is a 1999 publication, not a 1995 document.
img.credit: Cover of README! ASCII Culture and the Revenge of Knowledge, Filtered by Nettime (New York: Autonomedia, 1999). Monoskop.

body: Roman Verostko and Jean-Pierre Hébert founded “The Algorists,” along with Charles Csuri, Manfred Mohr, Mark Wilson and Ken Musgrave, to form a group based on the mutual adoration of the art that could be produced by algorithms. These were not artists new to the field but were a collection of artists who had dedicated decades, entire careers or lifetimes to the craft. Their work utilized algorithms for both form and social commentary but it was Hébert’s manifesto where he defined the term “algorist,” referring to artists who used algorithmic processes. Beyond plotted work, their influence extends to textiles, games, biological interfaces and experiments with evolutionary forms. It’s no surprise that artists formed around this time as the mid-1990s were marked by the widespread use of computers. In these conditions algorithmic art was flourishing, influencing a wide range of creative disciplines. Hebert and Verostko stand as two of the more under-appreciated pioneers of digital expression yet their legacy continues to this day through this special group.

img.cap: The two founders of the Algorists, Roman Verostko and Jean-Pierre Hébert, photographed together in Santa Barbara in 2011, as published on Verostko's algorists.org. It is a 2011 photograph, not a 1995 one.
img.credit: Roman Verostko (left) and Jean-Pierre Hébert (right), Santa Barbara, 2011. algorists.org.

body: The Slade Centre for Electronic Media in Fine Art (SCEMFA) was opened. The history of the department extends back to 1973 when Malcolm Hughes founded the Experimental Department at the Slade. Thus, the legacy of Hughes’s groundbreaking department continues to this very day. The Centre’s goal was to unite artists and researchers at the Slade School of Fine Art. It became a hub for exploring digital materials, fostering research into Electronic Media and Fine Art. Over the years, SCEMFA has played a vital role in shaping national and international dialogues on digital art, hosting events like Collision and Spontaneous Reaction.

body: In the early days of the public web, JODI emerged as pioneers of net art with their enigmatic website, begun around 1993, archived at wwwwwwwww.jodi.org. Their webpages, visually jarring and avant garde, challenged traditional site design norms. Navigation relied on cursor movements, with links hidden within repeated images. Some images led to new visual landscapes, blurring the lines between art and exploration. wwwwwwwww.jodi.org/ epitomized the experimental spirit of net art, offering a glimpse into the limitless possibilities of digital expression on the web. JODI’s work underscored the transformative power of the Internet as an art distribution mechanism, fitting into the long history of mass media art.
Fellow net.art pioneer Vuk Ćosić explained to the author (Peter Bauman) how in his view JODI were the first net.art practitioners:

“On the nettime list itself we didn’t post net.art pieces that could be displayed or collected but we spoke about it and gave it life. I personally adored the JODI posts that were consistently pushing the idea of net.art as a liberating force. They were the first in many regards.”

wwwwwwwww.jodi.org/ is not only socially critical but also self-reflexive work, commenting on the early Web while using the Internet itself as a canvas. The Internet gave artists the ability to self-publish their work to a global audience for the first time in human history. JODI’s early net art is a powerful demonstration of how the Internet would soon impact every art practice.

img.cap: A Netscape screen capture of JODI's Automatic Rain, one of the first works the pair published at jodi.org in 1995, with the address wwww.jodi.org/betalab/rain/auto.html visible in the location bar.
img.credit: JODI, Automatic Rain, 1995. Rhizome, Net Art Anthology.

body: Another example of early net art, Holger Friese’s Unendlich, fast... was a bold departure from the early internet landscape, which emphasized clarity and navigability. In contrast to the expected plethora of pages and links, Friese presented a single, enigmatic webpage. Visitors were greeted by a sea of vibrant blue, with only scroll bars for navigation. This minimalist space challenged conventions, encouraging interactivity, questions and exploration. It was an invitation to touch the art, using a webpage to play with point of view and perspective. At the center of the page to the right is a static image resembling stars in a vast cosmos. However, there are no clickable links or pathways to other destinations. Friese’s rejection of conventional navigation systems encourages visitors to embrace the unknown and seek meaning beyond traditional structures. The work encapsulates Friese’s rejection of imposed order, inviting users to navigate the infinite within the confines of a single, captivating space.

img.cap: A browser screenshot of Holger Friese's unendlich, fast..., showing the near-monochrome blue field with its cluster of tiny marks at right and the scrollbars that are the work's only navigation.
img.credit: Holger Friese, unendlich, fast..., 1995. Screenshot reproduced in Thomas Dreher, IASLonline Lektionen in NetArt, Ludwig-Maximilians-Universitat Munchen.

body: Nam June Paik’s Electronic Superhighway: Continental U.S., Alaska, Hawaii captured the United States’ shift into the information age in the mid-90s with the uncertainty and optimism that entailed. Paik’s work combined neon lights and video screens, illustrating the interconnectedness fostered by the rising Internet. Beyond its celebration of global communication, the piece prompts contemplation of technology’s encroaching cultural impact. The work’s scale evokes feelings of information overload, despite the still relativelyt small size of the mid-90s Internet. This work stands as one of Paik’s most well known, standing as a rare example of media art that garnered widespread attention, capturing the zeitgeist of society’s mid-90s relationship with a history-changing technology.

img.cap: Nam June Paik's fifty-one-channel video and neon map of the United States, in the Smithsonian American Art Museum's own photograph of the work.
img.credit: Nam June Paik, Electronic Superhighway: Continental U.S., Alaska, Hawaii, 1995. Smithsonian American Art Museum, Gift of the artist, 2002.23. © Nam June Paik Estate.

body: The Verbasizer is developed by David Bowie and Ty Roberts as a way to automate and speed up Bowie’s long-standing technique of cutting up fragments of text and rearranging them at random to create song lyrics.
-Sasha Stiles

img.cap: An animated GIF from Motherboard's report on the Verbasizer, showing the application's screen assembling randomised word strings such as 'top medals admiral'.
img.credit: Animated GIF from 'The Verbasizer Was David Bowie's 1995 Lyric-Writing Mac App', Motherboard (Vice), January 2016. Internet Archive Wayback Machine.

body: Larry Page and Sergey Brin met at Stanford in 1995 and formed their partnership the following year, when they built the search engine they called BackRub, running on Stanford’s servers. It laid the groundwork for what would become Google. By creating a powerful search engine algorithm, Page and Brin hoped to efficiently organize the vast amount of data on the internet. Their approach prioritized relevant search results, giving users a more intuitive and efficient way to find information. The birth of Google was a watershed moment in the digital age, where the rise of big data was only in its infancy. Google’s early entry into big data positioned it to become one of the world’s most valuable companies nearly thirty years later.

img.credit: Wikipedia. 2024. "Google." Wikimedia Foundation. Last modified March 6, 2024. en.wikipedia.org.

body: Another early work of virtual reality and interactive art that anticipated virtual worlds, Char Davies’s Osmose transported participants into a perception distorting realm. Participants could navigate various landscapes, from serene forests to subterranean realms, using a head-mounted display and abreath and balance-based motion tracking. Unlike traditional VR, Osmose used semi-representational, translucent visuals along with spatially multi-dimensional soundscapes to achieve a contemplative space. It invited participants to engage the body’s most basic functions—breathing and balance. The work explored how the digital affected our consciousness, anticipating the work of contemporary artists such as Lauren Lee McCarthy.

body: This “really significant work” in the rise of digital mass media art according to Casey Reas, Puppet Motel is an enigmatic CD-ROM by Laurie Anderson, designed with Hsin-Chien Huang and released on Voyager. With a blend of multimedia elements, including spoken word, video, music and computer graphics, Anderson crafts an immersive game-like experience that explores themes such as technology’s impact on time memory and human connection. Set within a series of interconnected scenes, the art-game invites participant-players to navigate through haunting environments, from monolithic rooms to surreal landscapes, each filled with snippets of art and conversation. Anderson’s distinctive voice echoes throughout, guiding players through the multimedia labyrinth. Back in 1995, Puppet Motel was posing poignant questions about the digital age, juxtaposing abstract spaces with tangible objects to evoke a sense of disconnection and longing for human connection. It’s Despite its complexity and darkness, the game maintains a playful spirit, inviting players to explore its depths and uncover its layers of meaning. Puppet Motel stands as a testament to Anderson’s approach to interactive art with the most cutting-edge technology of the time, the clunky CD-ROM, challenging players to confront the realities of existence in a continually digitizing world.

img.credit: Laurie Anderson with Huang Hsin-Chien, Puppet Motel, CD-ROM (New York: The Voyager Company, 1995). Scan from the Internet Archive CD-ROM preservation collection.

body: There is a legend that has persisted—for decades—that net.art was first coined by Vuk Ćosić from a garbled email. I spoke to to Ćosić about the claim, who debunked the legend but not for the first time: “First coinage: there is this legend that I received an e.mail with garbled text. False. That story itself is one of the better pieces of net.art, done by Alexei Shoulgin. It was widely repeated and for me it works as our take at the words such as Impressionism and Cubism that came from outside or Dada that came from inside but is foggy. The expression net.art was invented by Pit Schultz during our debates about online specific art, and we all liked it because .art was just like a file extension. Like .pdf or .doc.”

cite.label: Alexei Shulgin, “Net.Art - the origin,” nettime-l, March 18, 1997 (the original garbled-email story).
Rachel Greene, “Web Work: A History of Internet Art,” Artforum, May 2000 (repeats the origin legend).
Josephine Bosma, “A Net Artist Named Google: Alexei Shulgin and Josephine Bosma in Conversation,” Rhizome, January 12, 2017 (identifies the story as a prank).
Régine Debatty, “Interview of Vuk Cosic,” We Make Money Not Art, February 17, 2006 (Ćosić credits Pit Schultz with the term).
Vuk Ćosić, interview with Peter Bauman (author-supplied quotation).

body: December 19, 1996 marked the initial release of Macromedia Flash, a technology that paved the way rich graphics on the maturing web and for contemporary generative-web-based practices, pioneered by artists such as Joshua Davis, Yugo Nakamura, Brendan Dawes, James Paterson and LIA.

Flash, now a ubiquitous name in the annals of the web’s history, traces its roots back to a serendipitous meeting between Jonathan Gay and Charlie Jackson at a local Macintosh Users Group. Their 1993 brainchild, FutureWave Software, initially set its sights on pen computing. With the fading trend, they pivoted towards the burgeoning World Wide Web.

The culmination of their efforts was FutureSplash, a pioneering web animation tool released in May 1996. FutureSplash Animator empowered designers to craft animations with increased ease, while the accompanying FutureSplash Viewer allowed for playback on browsers.

When FutureSplash caught the attention of Netscape and Microsoft, its trajectory shifted dramatically. Netscape featured it as an extension, while Microsoft integrated it into MSN.com, catapulting FutureSplash into the public’s attention.
Recognizing its potential, Macromedia acquired FutureWave in December 1996, rebranding it as Macromedia Flash.

body: Another important example in the rise of Mass Media art, a Casey Reas precondition for NFTs, and net art, My boyfriend came back from the war by Olia Lialina is one of the most recognizable net art works. Russian artist Olia Lialina crafted My Boyfriend, a browser-based net-art piece consists of a nonlinear narrative using nested frames and grainy GIF images. The work’s interactive hypertext storytelling unfolds as users click hyperlinks, splitting the frame into smaller frames and revealing fragments of a couple’s reunion after a nameless military conflict. Lialina’s innovative use of frames within frames creates a mosaic-like experience, reminiscent of early silent movies. Lialina’s work, self-described as a “netfilm,” merges cinematic narrative techniques with HTML code, merging web and cinema. My Boyfriend stands as a significant example of art distributed solely through the Internet, showcasing Lialina’s mastery of spatial and temporal montage.

body: Rhizome begins: “Rhizome is the home of born-digital art and culture since 1996.” That 1996 start occurred when Mark Tribe founded Rhizome, initially as an email list that attracted some of the earliest artists exploring online mediums. Since its inception, Rhizome has been instrumental in shaping the trajectory of art intersecting with the internet and networked technologies. From its humble beginnings, Rhizome has evolved into a thriving non-profit organization affiliated with the New Museum. Today, its robust programs encompass a wide range of initiatives aimed at supporting and preserving artistic practices that engage with technology. It remains an important repository for early net art, especially.

body: Despite initiating the project in June 1991, on January 23, 1996, JavaSoft, the newly formed operating company of Sun Microsystems, released Java 1.0, marking a significant milestone in the history of software development. Java 1.0 introduced the “write-once-run-everywhere” capability, enabling developers and artists to create platform-independent applications and algorithms. With components like the Java Applet Viewer and class libraries included, Java 1.0 quickly gained traction in the software and internet communities. Its widespread adoption by companies like IBM and Netscape solidified its position as the de facto standard for networked applications, shaping the future of software development as well as creative expression with code. The release of Java is particularly important to digital generative art’s history as the Processing creative coding language used the Java language.

body: John Maeda’s arrival at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) in 1996 marked a pivotal moment in the intersection of technology, design and art. As the founder of the Aesthetics + Computation Group (ACG), an evolution of Visible Language Workshop, Maeda continued the exploration of how computation could enhance graphic design, initiated by Muriel Cooper in 1975. Under Maeda’s leadership, the ACG scrutinized the possibilities of code as a medium for expression, laying the groundwork for the development of innovative tools like Processing. Collaborators Ben Fry and Casey Reas, inspired by Maeda’s vision, began crafting Processing in 2001 as a simplified environment for coding, bridging the gap between programming and design. This endeavor continues to greatly impact the broader culture today, as the Processing Foundation and Lauren Lee McCarthy would go on to develop p5.js.

body: With Traffic at Bordeaux’s CAPC Contemporary Museum, Nicolas Bourriaud introduced his concept of 'relational aesthetics,' art that serves as “a vehicle for creating encounters between the artist and the viewers, the latter of which is ideally involved as an active participant.” The exhibition matters for this timeline because it stands as an example of the digital’s concerns manifested in the mainstream art world. These concerns include interactivity, the removing distinctions between art and everyday life and an inclusive definition of what art can entail.

body: The Crossing by Bill Viola showcases his pioneering use of video technologies since the 1970s. Viola’s early experiments with portable recording devices evolved into immersive installations, featuring multi-channel displays that envelop viewers in meticulously crafted visuals, often set within darkened environments.

body: Alexei Shulgin’s Form Art is c3.hu of net art that explores the HTML language’s potential as a medium for artistic expression. Shulgin uses playful manipulation and repetition of basic HTML elements to create visually dynamic and ever-changing compositions that were meant to be interpreted as challenges to traditional notions of art in the rising idea of the digital age that was taking hold in the mid-90s. Society was coming to terms on a mass level that we could no longer afford to fear or slow digitization. Art began reflecting this slow coming to terms and that included net art in general. Form Art received an honorary mention at the 1997 Ars Electronica.

body: Documenta Done by the net art pioneer Vuk Ćosić subverts institutional control over net art’s circulation, epitomizing the artist’s role as a digital pirate. Born from the controversial decision to sell the documenta X website as a CD-ROM, Ćosić's work of art was an interpreted at the time as an act of artistic piracy. The work involved copying, republishing and circulating the site, framing it as a major international art theft. Serving both as critique and archival intervention, Documenta Done underscores the challenges institutions face in preserving digital culture’s social memory. Despite its provocative origins, the project has evolved into a vital artifact of the net.art period, continuing to provoke discourse on the intersection of art, technology, and institutional power.

img.cap: A Netscape screen capture of Vuk Cosic's Documenta Done, showing the copied documenta X homepage republished at ljudmila.org/~vuk/dx/, with the original documenta X credits intact.
img.credit: Vuk Cosic, Documenta Done, 1997. Rhizome, Net Art Anthology.

body: Karl Sims continued to pioneer evolutionary art with his work Galápagos, blending audience interaction with computational evolution. Viewers could influence the survival and reproduction of virtual organisms by selecting preferred forms via step sensor pads. Sims' approach combined genetics, neural networks and physics simulations to create lifelike animations based on Darwinian evolution. Sims’s use of of plant-like abstract imagery and virtual creatures demonstrated how algorithmic art could contribute to the fields of artificial and evolutionary life and their impact on emergent systems. This work was first displayed at the ICC in Tokyo from 1997 to 2000.

Sims like Primordial Dance earlier in the decade is using evolutionary principles to recreate what is essentially a slightly more manual GAN process. In Galapagos, Sims increases the complexity of Dance by including audience participation and including an immersive environment. There is a clear connection between the AI of today and Sims’s work, as he explains his process in this piece himself:

“Twelve computers simulate the growth and behaviors of a population of abstract animated forms and display them on twelve screens arranged in an arc. The viewers participate in this exhibit by selecting which organisms they find most aesthetically interesting and standing on step sensors in front of those displays. The selected organisms survive, mate, mutate and reproduce.”

This evolutionary work of Sims can be considered proto-AI art. Artists in the upcoming decades would continue to automate the process until now these tasks are done “under the hood” and instantly. But this is a hugely important step in the development of AI-art-as-we-know-it-today.

To further display how instrumental this work has been in the development of contemporaneous AI-art, in 1999, Scott Draves’s legendary early AI-art was inspired by the immersive, gallery-bound approach of Sims’s Galapagos.

img.credit: Courtesy of Karl Sims. karlsims.com

body: This cultural facility in Tokyo, dedicated to exploring the intersections of art, science, and technology, has been instrumental in creating a platform for generative art in Japan. Since opening, it has held exhibitions and a variety of programs while publishing a journal to expose the public to new media art. Karl Sims exhibited work here from 1997-2000 and Golan Levin and Zach Lieberman exhibited their interactive work here in 2007.

body: Feng Mengbo’s My Private Album was a pioneering work of interactive CD-ROM art, examining the combination of digital storytelling and interactivity. The work provides viewers with a dynamic look at how families change and evolve over time, questioning the concept of our family as static. Feng’s work deviates from conventional linear narratives, allowing audiences to interact choose their own path also integrating the complex nature of memory. Feng captures the essence of human resilience and hope in his art, which transcends aestheticism through intimate reflections on the ordinary lives of people. Carefully and humbly put together, My Private Album elevates the commonplace to the extraordinary, offering a moving audiovisual record that is available to everyone. It’s a standout of mid-90s interactive CD-ROM art.

img.cap: A screen from Feng Mengbo's interactive work My Private Album, showing a 1930s studio photograph of the artist's grandmother captioned in the work's own interface, with Menu and Quit buttons at lower left.

body: This immersive art project used the CAVE, developed by Carolina Cruz-Neira, Daniel J. Sandin and Thomas A. DeFanti at the Electronic Visualization Laboratory, University of Illinois at Chicago. The CAVE is a room-sized, surround-screen, projection-based virtual reality environment. The year prior in 1996, At the Ars Electronica Center in Austria, EVL set up the first CAVE that was open to the public and showcased several virtual reality artworks. World Skin, by Maurice Benayoun with the composer Jean-Baptiste Barrière, made an immersive space for participants to embark on a haunting “photo safari” through landscapes of warfare. Awarded the Golden Nica Prize for Interactive Art in 1998, the installation confronted viewers with a compilation of visceral images from battle zones, inviting them to intervene by capturing fragments of this grim reality with cameras. Each photographed moment was replaced by a black silhouette, symbolizing the extinguishing of a piece of the world. Through this poignant exploration, World Skin grappled with the significance of media images in shaping our perception of global conflicts, highlighting the paradox of how images simultaneously reveal and neutralize the rawness of human suffering. The work underscores the importance of concept and digital art that spoke to contemporary societal issues beyond simply celebrating technology.

body: Cities on the Move: Contemporary Asian Art at the Turn of the 21st Century” in Vienna, Austria, was the first presentation of a traveling exhibition curated by Hans Ulrich Obrist and Hou Hanru. Emerging against the backdrop of East Asia’s rapid urbanization, the exhibition went beyond traditional art displays, incorporating visual art, architecture and film to depict the cultural ramifications of the region’s urban development. With over 150 contributors, it took place in a variety of global venues, including MoMA PS1 in New York and the Hayward Gallery in London. But the first iteration took place in Vienna.

body: For the purposes of this Timeline, this event stands as tremendously more important than perhaps it should on first glance, as it marks the transition to the usage of the term of “generative art” as we understand and use it today. Previously, the movement was much more frequently called computer or algorithmic art. This is conference is an important step in the transition to and popularization of the term “generative art.”

Milan hosted said inaugural Generative Art conference, spearheaded by Celestino Soddu with Enrica Colabella. The event, which continues to this day, convened architects, mathematicians, poets and artists, uniting diverse disciplines under the banner of generative design. With discussions ranging from universal visual grammar to digital art, the conference aimed to spark enthusiasm for the generative process as understood in a more general way. This broader understanding of the generative is what makes the conference important. Soddu explains in the proceedings introduction:

“The Generative Art is a way to think and to design. Following this approach we can find, united by the same enthusiasm, architects and mathematicians, poets and musicians, physicists and semiothics, philosophers and painters, engineers and designers.”

Soddu and collaborators envision an annual gathering to further explore this interdisciplinary frontier. The conference proceedings, published with unique covers, mark a milestone in the evolution of generative art, affirming its status as a vibrant field of creative inquiry.

body: This now legendary piece of software was begun by Levin at the Interval Research Corporation in 1998 and completed at MIT in 1999 and 2000. He would go on to show this piece to John Maeda, which would convince Maeda to let Levin join MIT’s Aesthetics and Computation Group (ACG) the following year. Once there, Yellowtail, which was conceived before Maeda even created DBN, “was first implemented using the EasyDraw DirectDraw framework by Scott Snibbe; then the ACU C++ graphics framework by the MIT ACG, and then in the Processing Java framework by Ben Fry and Casey Reas.” The work, beyond getting Levin in MIT, also was one of the first to be tested in the legendary development of Processing at MIT in the mid-to-late-’90s. This work’s place in art history is secured.
Levin spoke to this author, Peter Bauman, about his work in the 1990s saying:

“My work from the late-90s was a reaction to the making culture that assumed that multimedia was constructed from preloaded assets like sprites and background images. I was like, ‘No, the computer is a dynamic medium that can generate things on the fly.’”

The piece itself is an interactive software work that transforms user gestures into dynamic, abstract animations. Strokes made by the user are looped continuously, allowing control over both the shape and movement quality of lines. Each line has its unique cycle, creating a fluid, responsive animation, resembling organic textures.

img.cap: Output from Golan Levin's Yellowtail: white animated gesture-marks looping across a black field, the tapering strokes the software generates from a drawn gesture.
img.credit: Golan Levin, Yellowtail, 1998-2000. Courtesy the artist, flong.com.

body: This pioneering work of net.art transforms a newspaper article about Heath Bunting, the artist, into a hyperlinked guide, where each word links to a corresponding website. Initially leading to dead ends in 1998, the project highlighted the commercialization of online visibility, as banal words led to purchased domain sites. Through this hypertext exploration, Bunting explored how Internet perception structures ownership conditions, exposing the ruins of the grand narrative as the foundation of the new economy. This project anticipated the blockchain and NFT’s contemporary exploration of ownership.

body: A classic of net. art, SHREDDER was a challenge to traditional print metaphors, embracing the web’s digita, data-based nature. potatoland.org transforms web pages into digital confetti, scattering markup, text, and images across the screen in a form of digital Abstract Expressionism. SHREDDER even gained the attention of the NY Times, showcasing how net.art was beginning to go mainstream at the end of the decade.

body: An important step in the rise of Mass Media Art, an important pre-condition for NFTs, according to Casey Reas, in October 1998, the MPEG (Moving Picture Experts Group) announced the MPEG-4 standard, ISO/IEC 14496, following the success of MPEG-1 and MPEG-2. This global effort involved hundreds of researchers and engineers, resulting in approval of an International Standard by early 1999. Importantly, the fully backward compatible MPEG-4 Version 2 extensions followed, extending capabilities for digital television, interactive graphics and multimedia applications for the early web. Critical to the rise of Madd Media Art, the standard facilitated the integration of production, distribution and content access. It thus laid the foundation for interactive video, CD-ROMs and digital television and their use in creative expression. Further extensions continued into the upcoming decades, ensuring ongoing advancements in multimedia technology.

body: Flash creative coder pioneer Joshua Davis released ps0.praystation.v0, his website for exhibiting experimental design and art using code, specifically Flash. The site also served as an important community resource for open source code. As a place for artists to both exhibit and learn, praystation.com was critical in the development of the intersection of the Internet, digital art and Mass Media art.

body: According to Tom White, ACU, a key predecessor of Processing formed in 1998. Before Processing, MIT’s Aesthetics and Computation Group (ACG) was already innovating, with the ACU toolkit, a C++ and OpenGL-based precursor that underpinned screen-based projects within the Aesthetics and Computation Group from 1999 to 2002. Preceding iterations like acWorlds and acJava paved the path, while echoes of earlier projects, such as Bob Sabiston’s “BadWindows” in the vlw era, reverberated through its development. ACU, in particular, provided a foundational structure for interactive graphics research, fueling endeavors in dynamic typography, visual programming systems, audio-visual environments and information visualization. ACU was thus a key pre-Processeing MIT ACG development.
