body: This book chapter, “Frankensteinian Methods for Evolutionary Music Composition,” by Peter Todd and Gregory Werner looks at co-evolutionary techniques in music composition. The pair aimed to create intelligent algorithmic music composition systems, inspired by the story of Frankenstein. The duo explains in their own words:

”[Our] approach involves separate populations of critic agents and composer agents, striving to establish a consistent aesthetic within a simulated culture. However, while their method yielded a coherent aesthetic, it often diverged from human sensibilities.”
In other words, they created a novel, cybernetic-feedback loop method for refining musical compositions that combined rules, learning and evolution, published in Musical Networks (MIT Press, 1999).

body: In surely one of generative art’s most legendary moments, John Maeda published Design By Numbers, with the aim of simplifying programming for artists and designers at the MIT Media Lab’s Aesthetics and Computation Group. Its minimalist interface and intuitive design enabled users to experiment with computational creativity, inspiring a new generation of digital artists and toolmakers to further fine tune and expand. The system’s simplified distribution and user-friendly syntax enabled workshops and courses at MIT and elsewhere. Benjamin Fry built DBN 2 and 3 and Casey Reas the courseware, gathering invaluable feedback, laying the groundwork for future improvements, eventually evolving into Processing. Golan Levin, an ACG student around this time, spoke to me about DBN:

“Processing grew out of Design by Numbers (DBN), which Zach’s current graduate student, Lingdong Huang, who was also my former student, just got working online. You can actually now play with DBN in the browser. This was announced only in October 2023. Now you can actually see projects that Casey Reas, Ben Fry and I made some twenty-odd years ago. DBN was John Maeda’s concept. And it allowed you to do interactive, computational and generative form on a canvas that had very specific limitations. And John is like the ultimate Bauhaus guy in terms of really liking simplicity and stark limitations. With DBN, you were limited to grayscale; you were limited to a canvas that was 100 x 100 pixels. It was kind of like a no-fun zone because you couldn’t make stuff that’s full of sexy colors. That’s because it was specifically a pedagogical tool.

‍‍Casey and Ben were like, “Yeah, this is great but we actually want to make art bigger than 100 pixels.” And John was like, “Well, that’s your business. If you want to make things that are colorful, artsy, big and whatever, go ahead.” Casey and Ben wanted to make an actually useful tool and not just a conceptual learning environment. They started working on it close to the time that I was graduating so I didn’t have a lot of direct involvement in it. But Yellowtail, for example, has been a demo in Processing since 2000. They looked to me to provide examples like that sometimes. I was probably one of the very first people to teach with it, other than Casey and Ben themselves.”

body: Described as a “collective intelligence,” this early example of machine learning in art was inspired by the evolutionary art work of Karl Sims. Scott Draves’s software art Electric Sheep is a distributed screen-saver-as-art and pivotal advancement in AI, artificial life and fractal art that originated from the Fractal Flame algorithm. Electric Sheep leveraged a distributed system with a client/server architecture, transforming computer screensavers into dynamic, networked canvases for fractal animations. Each “sheep” in the system consisted of 128 frames and a genetic code defined by 160 floating-point numbers.

An early AI-driven art project, Electric Sheep enlisted 450,000 participants globally, pioneering machine learning art and AI. The Flame algorithm mirrors contemporary neural networks' vector floating point approach. The collaborative rendering system allows computers worldwide to contribute, guided by human votes for the fittest animations. Each computer follows Draves' Flame algorithm to create a segment of the collective artwork. Open source and constantly evolving with contributions, Electric Sheep showcases family trees and resemblance through electricsheep.org. Draves serves as head Shepherd, overseeing this dynamic, participatory project in AI-driven art.

body: The renowned net art duo JODI’s release of SOD represented a blend of their net.art roots, video game art and the video game cracking culture that led to the demoscene. The work is a warped, scrambled version of “Wolfenstein3D” (1992), a game chosen for “its ‘abandonware’ status,” as the game was seven years old in 1999, according to Phillipa Stalker.

A participator from the time was quoted as saying, “Every ‘wall’ of the maze is rendered in black and white geometric patterns, while the main enemy in the game appears as two inverted triangles.” Despite this graphical reduction and intentional obfuscation, gameplay remarkably remains intact. JODI invites viewers to become active participators in a world of their own creation, making SOD not only a unique digital expression capturing the late ’90s gaming and internet culture, but also a journey into JODI’s surreal vision of the world.

body: Another important example of net.art and the rise of Mass Media art that was popularizing around the end of the decade, LIA’s Re-move (1999–2003) explores generative-audiovisual compositions that combine organic forms “with the rawness of fin-de-siècle Viennese abstraction.”

These works were originally created in Macromedia Director and released “on the internet to be accessible by everyone,” the artist told author Peter Bauman. They were also later released on CD-ROM. The work has since been restored for the Net Art Anthology. Each composition in Re-move achieves a delicate balance between the artist’s formal choices, user interaction, chance and algorithmic processes.

These elements emphasizes the computer’s role as a dynamic medium rather than a static device. By balancing responsiveness, randomness and repetition, the time-based abstractions maintain legibility amidst their intricate complexity. Casey Reas mentions the Macromedia Director work of LIA, released on CD-ROM, as important experimental work of this time.

This pioneering work of Flash art and net.art by Auriea Harvey and Michaël Samyn, skinonskinonskin, was a collection of the pair’s digital love letters. Initially shared privately, the two turned the letters into interactive web pages—which included Flash animations, audio, text and images. They were later made available to paid subscribers as online artwork. The project typifies the decade-long rise of mass-media art, looking at the intersection of artistic collaboration and romantic connection in the digital age.

Harvey and Samyn’s shared practice, Entropy8Zuper!, merged their individual artistry, blurring the lines between their personal and professional lives. skinonskinonskin challenged traditional notions of the cold digital and how humans displayed intimacy, anticipating the Internet’s impact on romantic relationships and dating apps in the twenty-first century. The piece invited viewers to feel a touch that transcended physical space, symbolizing a profound connection through the internet’s newly laid wires.

body: Firmly in what many believe is the Web3 era, this nomenclature was first developed over twenty years prior. Darcy DiNucci coined the term “Web 2.0” in her article “Fragmented Future” for Print magazine. The designation was meant to underscore the Web fragmenting across devices as a transport layer. Web 2.0 includes early social networking platforms, forums, wikis and multimedia sharing sites such as Joshua Davis’s praystation.v0. Tim O’Reilly and Dale Dougherty popularized the term even further in 2004 when they hosted a Web 2.0 conference.

body: Based on custom software he developed in 1996 and released in 1998, according to DAM, Ćosić’s Raging Bull and Deep ASCII were some of the first ASCII films, as all the visuals are reduced to green ASCII characters. Deep ASCII was first and with a running time of fifty-five minutes recreates the pornographic film with ASCII characters. Knowing this was likely a first, the work stands as punk nod to Ćosić’s net.art roots. The works also may have influenced the aesthetics for the Matrix and many other “hacker” portraying films of the time and their use animated binary code in green with a black background. The work asks questions about what is lost when we send messages within a digital context.

body: The Flash 4 savant Nakamura originally launched yugop.com in 1999. The Flash-based site demonstrated a masterful blend of simplicity and interactivity that would influence the trajectory of art and design on the web. MoMA even used Nakamura’s design firm for the bespoke page for the Paola Antonelli curated, Design and the Elastic Mind website. moma.org:

“Paola Antonelli, the exhibition curator, had gone through around twenty links from three firms when we showed her Yugo Nakamura’s personal site, yugop.com. The simple white page that greeted us was immediately invaded by dark, two-dimensional cascading balls. We watched for a few minutes, mesmerized by the simple physics of bouncing. Paola decided to go with Yugo’s firm, tha.jp, on the spot.”
He was one of the contributing authors of New Masters of Flash (friends of ED, 2000).
